item.text: {"question_id":"4B.6","answer":"In 2023, independent media and internet access remained active: law formally protected expression, press freedom, access to information, and internet access, and there was no documented nationwide blocking or filtering. However, López Obrador and officials repeatedly stigmatized journalists through presidential briefings, while progovernment accounts conducted smear campaigns, including the March 2023 attack on Supreme Court president Norma Piña. Publicly funded InfodemiaMX and the “Who’s Who in Lies” segment were reported as presenting biased or false information. The administration also failed to establish transparent state-advertising rules; ten media and communication companies received 45.05 percent of the 2023 official advertising budget, creating financial dependence, though concentration alone does not prove editorial control. Access-to-information safeguards weakened when INAI lacked a quorum and nearly 6,000 cases accumulated, amid López Obrador and allied calls to dissolve the body, although the Supreme Court later enabled limited operation. Journalists also faced severe criminal violence, official and nonstate harassment, self-censorship, and impunity; responsibility for criminal-group violence is not established as personal responsibility of López Obrador, but RSF attributed insufficient reforms to his government. Surveillance allegations involving military-linked Pegasus operations and the government’s denials or minimization further undermined the information environment, although attribution and implementation are not fully adjudicated. A proposed April 2023 cybersecurity law contained serious potential content-regulation, takedown, criminalization, privacy, and militarization risks, but it had not been enacted by the end of the reporting period and therefore is evidence of proposed risk, not implemented censorship.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E014","BATCH-0014-E003","BATCH-0014-E004","BATCH-0026-E016","BATCH-0026-E020","BATCH-0044-E012","BATCH-0051-E019"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0014-E001","BATCH-0014-E006","BATCH-0026-E013","BATCH-0026-E015","BATCH-0026-E018","BATCH-0057-E007"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Some Freedom House evidence covers June 2022–May 2023 or June 2023–May 2024 rather than the full calendar year; personal presidential responsibility for those crimes is not established.","Formal legal safeguards and court rulings show contrary protective evidence, but do not demonstrate consistently effective de facto protection."],"corrections_made":["Separated direct 2023 evidence from partial, overlapping, inherited, and retrospective evidence.","Added the omitted 2023 evidence on progovernment online networks, the Norma Piña smear campaign, InfodemiaMX, and the presidential “Who’s Who in Lies” segment.","Recast the cybersecurity proposal as an unenacted projected risk rather than an implemented restriction.","Preserved the distinction between formal protections, operational pressure, outcomes, and uncertain attribution.","Qualified the role of criminal violence, surveillance allegations, advertising concentration, and INAI deterioration without treating them as conclusively personal acts by López Obrador."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["A full rejudgment would benefit from calendar-year 2023 quantitative evidence on journalist attacks, killings, self-censorship, government advertising allocation, and INAI case handling.","The evidentiary record would benefit from adjudicated findings on military surveillance authorization, government or party financing of online networks, and the practical enforcement of information-access and media rules."]}
